transitivity: both — transitive (*dress* the baby), intransitive (he *dresses* well)
gloss: To put clothes on yourself or on another person.
examples: He *dresses* for the weather, not for the office.
She *dressed* the twins in matching coats.
I was *dressing* when the phone rang.
contrast: About yourself Americans say *get dressed*, not *dress myself*: I got dressed in five minutes.

gloss: To take clothes off yourself or off another person.
examples: The nurse asked him to *undress* behind the curtain.
She *undressed* the sleepy child and put him to bed.
He had already *undressed* and was half asleep.

gloss: To put on different clothes, or to put different clothes on someone.
examples: I need to *change* before dinner.
She *changed* into jeans the moment she got home.
He is *changing* the baby in the back room.
contrast: The final *e* drops before *-ing*: *changing*. You change **into** clothes, not *change on*.

gloss: To take something off the body or out of a place.
examples: Please *remove* your shoes at the door.
He *removed* his hat and shook the snow off it.
The price tag has been *removed*, so I cannot return it.
contrast: *Remove* is the formal word; in ordinary speech Americans say *take off*.

gloss: To put on a piece of clothing or equipment.
examples: Firefighters *don* full gear before they go in.
She *donned* a white coat and walked into the lab.
He was *donning* his uniform when the alarm sounded.
contrast: The *n* doubles: *don → donned, donning*. This verb belongs to writing; in speech people say *put on*.

gloss: To put clothing on or take it off with one quick, easy movement.
examples: Give me a second to *slip* into something warmer.
She *slipped* the ring off her finger and set it down.
He was *slipping* his arms into the sleeves as he walked.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *slip → slipped, slipping*. You slip **into** or **out of** clothes.

gloss: To take off all your clothes, or to pull a covering off something.
examples: The kids *strip* the second they see the pool.
He *stripped* to the waist and kept digging.
She was *stripping* the beds when I got there.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *strip → stripped, stripping*.

gloss: To put clothing or cloth over a part of the body.
examples: *Cover* your shoulders before you go inside.
She *covered* her head with a thin scarf.
His arms were *covered* to the wrist.
contrast: You cover something **with** a scarf, a coat, a blanket.

ru: одеваться слоями, надевать одно на другое
gloss: To wear or put on several pieces of clothing one over another.
examples: In March you just have to *layer*.
She *layered* a vest over her sweater.
He is *layering* a flannel shirt under his jacket.

gloss: To hang cloth loosely over someone or something.
examples: *Drape* the scarf over one shoulder and leave it.
He *draped* his coat across the back of the chair.
A wool blanket was *draped* over her knees.
contrast: The *e* drops before *-ing*: *draping*.

gloss: To decorate a person or an object, especially with jewelry or ornament.
examples: Tiny pearls *adorn* the collar and the cuffs.
She *adorned* her hair with fresh flowers.
The robe was *adorned* with gold thread.
contrast: You adorn something **with** something else.

gloss: To add belts, jewelry, scarves, or bags to an outfit.
examples: She knows how to *accessorize*.
He *accessorized* the gray suit with a green tie.
The dress is plain, so it can be *accessorized* any way you like.
contrast: American spelling takes *-ize*; British writing often has *accessorise*.

gloss: To change clothes or appearance so that people do not recognize you.
examples: A wig alone will not *disguise* you.
He *disguised* himself as a delivery driver.
She was *disguised* in a long coat and dark glasses.
contrast: The *s* in the middle is a /z/ sound and the *u* is silent: dis-GYZ.

gloss: To cover the face, or to hide something from view.
examples: A bandana will *mask* the lower half of your face.
The dancers *masked* their faces for the last scene.
Every one of the riders was *masked*.

gloss: To cover the face or head with a thin cloth.
examples: Traditional dress *veils* the hair and the neck.
She *veiled* her face before entering the shrine.
The window was *veiled* with pale lace.
contrast: *Veil* sounds exactly like *vale*, an old word for a valley.

gloss: To supply someone with the clothes or equipment they need.
examples: The school *outfits* every player with a uniform.
They *outfitted* the whole crew in orange vests.
The store is *outfitting* the entire wedding party.
contrast: The *t* doubles: *outfit → outfitted, outfitting*.

gloss: To wrap a baby tightly in a cloth or a light blanket.
examples: Nurses *swaddle* newborns to keep them calm.
She *swaddled* the baby and laid him in the crib.
He is *swaddling* her for the night.

gloss: To wrap someone in warm clothes, or to tie things together in a bunch.
examples: *Bundle* the kids in their snow gear before they go out.
She *bundled* the baby in two blankets.
The old sweaters were *bundled* and carried to the attic.

gloss: To put clothing on for a moment to see whether it fits or looks right.
examples: Ask whether you can *try* the next size up.
She *tried* three jackets and bought none of them.
He is *trying* the boots in a wider width.
contrast: The *y* becomes *i*: *try → tries, tried*, but *trying* keeps the *y*. In a store Americans add *on*: *try on a coat*.

gloss: To wear something noticeable and look pleased about it.
examples: He likes to *sport* a bow tie at weddings.
She *sported* bright red boots all winter.
The whole team was *sporting* new warm-up jackets.
contrast: This verb has nothing to do with games; *sport* meaning a game is only a noun.

gloss: To close a piece of clothing with buttons, a zipper, or a clasp.
examples: The coat *fastens* at the shoulder.
She *fastened* the top button and went in.
He was *fastening* his watch strap in the elevator.
contrast: The *t* is silent: FAS-uhn, like *listen* and *soften*.

gloss: To open something that is buttoned, buckled, or zipped.
examples: Do not *unfasten* your seat belt yet.
He *unfastened* his collar and loosened his tie.
She had *unfastened* only two buttons.
contrast: The *t* is silent here too: un-FAS-uhn.

gloss: To close a shirt, coat, or jacket with its buttons.
examples: *Button* your coat, it is freezing out there.
He *buttoned* the shirt wrong and had to start over.
She is *buttoning* her daughter's sweater.
contrast: The final *n* does not double, because the stress is on the first syllable: *buttoned*, *buttoning*.

gloss: To open a shirt or coat by undoing its buttons.
examples: He *unbuttons* his cuffs whenever he works.
She *unbuttoned* her coat in the warm room.
His shirt was *unbuttoned* at the neck.

gloss: To close something with a zipper.
examples: This jacket *zips* all the way to the chin.
She *zipped* her bag and ran for the bus.
He is *zipping* the kids into their snowsuits.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *zip → zipped, zipping*. Americans call the fastener a *zipper*.

gloss: To open a zipper.
examples: *Unzip* the lining and pull it out.
He *unzipped* his hoodie and sat down.
The tent had been *unzipped* from the inside.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *unzip → unzipped, unzipping*.

gloss: To fasten a belt, a shoe, or a strap with a buckle.
examples: *Buckle* the strap under his chin.
She *buckled* her sandals and stood up.
He was *buckling* the belt on the last notch.

gloss: To undo a buckle.
examples: Wait until the plane stops to *unbuckle* your belt.
He *unbuckled* his sandals at the door.
She had already *unbuckled* the child from the car seat.

gloss: To pull laces through the holes of a shoe or boot and tie them.
examples: *Lace* the boots tight before a long hike.
He *laced* his skates in a hurry.
She knelt on the step, *lacing* her running shoes.
contrast: The verb *lace* and *lace*, the delicate fabric, are spelled and said the same way.

gloss: To fasten something with a knot or a bow.
examples: He can *tie* his own shoes now.
She *tied* the sash in a neat bow.
The apron was *tied* so loosely that it came undone.
contrast: The *-ing* form changes its spelling: *tie → tying*, never *tieing*.

gloss: To undo a knot or a bow.
examples: *Untie* the apron and hang it on the hook.
He *untied* his boots out on the porch.
She was *untying* the ribbon as carefully as she could.
contrast: Same spelling change as *tie*: *untying*, not *untieing*.

gloss: To tie something into a knot.
examples: *Knot* the ends of the scarf together.
He *knotted* his tie in front of the mirror.
The laces were *knotted* so tightly that I had to cut them.
contrast: The *k* is silent and the *t* doubles: *knot → knotted, knotting*. It sounds exactly like *not*.

gloss: To fasten a necklace, a bracelet, or a bag with its clasp.
examples: Can you *clasp* this necklace for me?
She *clasped* the bracelet around her wrist.
The purse is *clasped* with a small brass catch.

gloss: To fasten something with a hook, or to hang it on one.
examples: *Hook* the top of the dress first, then zip it.
She *hooked* the strap and pulled the zipper up.
His jacket was *hooked* over the back of the chair.

gloss: To undo something that is fastened with a hook.
examples: *Unhook* the collar if it feels too tight.
He *unhooked* the coat from the peg by the door.
The belt had been *unhooked* and left on the chair.

gloss: To hold something in place with a strap.
examples: *Strap* the helmet under your chin.
She *strapped* the baby into the carrier.
The sandals are *strapped* around the ankle.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *strap → strapped, strapping*.

gloss: To push the edge of a piece of clothing inside or under something.
examples: *Tuck* your shirt into your pants.
He *tucked* the label back inside the collar.
Her jeans were *tucked* into tall boots.

gloss: To pull a belt or a cord tight around something.
examples: *Cinch* the coat at the waist with a wide belt.
She *cinched* the dress and it looked like a different dress.
The hood is *cinched* with a drawstring.
contrast: It ends in *-ch*, so the third person adds *-es*: *cinches*.

gloss: To take off a part that is made to come off.
examples: The hood *detaches* with two snaps.
He *detached* the liner from his winter coat.
The straps can be *detached* and washed separately.
contrast: It ends in *-ch*, so the third person adds *-es*: *detaches*.

gloss: To pass something long around or through in the shape of a loop.
examples: *Loop* the belt through every belt loop, not just the front ones.
She *looped* the scarf twice around her neck.
The cord is *looped* over the hook behind the door.

gloss: To fasten clothing with the small metal fasteners that click shut.
examples: The jacket *snaps* instead of zipping.
She *snapped* the cuffs closed and pulled on her gloves.
The hood is *snapped* onto the collar.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *snap → snapped, snapping*.

gloss: To fold and sew the bottom edge of a piece of cloth.
examples: The tailor can *hem* them by Friday.
She *hemmed* the curtains herself in one evening.
These pants have been *hemmed* twice already.
contrast: The *m* doubles: *hem → hemmed, hemming*.

gloss: To repair a hole in knitted cloth by sewing back and forth across it.
examples: My grandmother could *darn* a sock in ten minutes.
He *darned* the elbow of his old sweater.
She sat by the window, *darning* socks.

gloss: To sew a decorative pattern onto cloth with colored thread.
examples: She likes to *embroider* in the evenings.
They *embroidered* his initials on the pocket.
The jacket is *embroidered* with red flowers.

gloss: To make cloth by looping yarn with a single hook.
examples: She is teaching me to *crochet*.
He *crocheted* a blanket for the baby.
She is *crocheting* a hat for winter.
contrast: The final *t* is silent: kroh-SHAY. The past *crocheted* is said kroh-SHAYD.

gloss: To sew two layers of cloth together with padding between them.
examples: They *quilt* together every Thursday afternoon.
She *quilted* the lining by hand.
He wore a *quilted* vest under his coat.

gloss: To come apart into loose threads, or to pull knitted work apart on purpose.
examples: Cheap sweaters *unravel* after one season.
The whole sleeve *unraveled* from one loose thread.
She is *unraveling* the old scarf to reuse the yarn.
contrast: American spelling keeps one *l*: *unraveled, unraveling*; British writing doubles it.

gloss: To catch cloth on something sharp and pull a thread loose.
examples: Rings *snag* fine knits every time.
She *snagged* her tights on the corner of the desk.
He kept *snagging* the sweater on the drawer handle.
contrast: The *g* doubles: *snag → snagged, snagging*.

gloss: To fold cloth into regular flat folds and sew them in place.
examples: They *pleat* the fabric before attaching the waistband.
She *pleated* the skirt by hand.
He wore a *pleated* shirt with his tuxedo.

gloss: To pull cloth together into small soft folds with a thread.
examples: *Gather* the fabric evenly along the seam.
She *gathered* the waist with a band of elastic.
The sleeves are *gathered* at the shoulder.

gloss: To gather cloth into a strip of soft folds, or to push something out of its neat shape.
examples: The wind *ruffles* her skirt every time she crosses the bridge.
She *ruffled* the hem with a wide band of lace.
His hair was *ruffled* and his tie was crooked.

gloss: To make something longer, or to become longer.
examples: Can you *lengthen* the sleeves by an inch?
She *lengthened* the dress by letting down the hem.
The straps have been *lengthened* as far as they go.

gloss: To cover the inside of a coat, a bag, or a box with another material.
examples: They *line* the winter coats with flannel.
She *lined* the jacket with cheap silk.
The boots are *lined* with wool.
contrast: You line something **with** a material, and the inner layer itself is the *lining*.

gloss: To turn the bottom of a sleeve or a pant leg up into a fold.
examples: He likes to *cuff* his jeans above his boots.
She *cuffed* the sleeves of his big sweater twice.
The pants came back *cuffed* and pressed.

ru: шить на заказ, подгонять по фигуре, подогнать
gloss: To make or alter clothes so that they fit one person exactly.
examples: A good shop will *tailor* the suit to your measurements.
They *tailored* the jacket in two days.
The coat is beautifully *tailored*.
contrast: You tailor a garment **to** a person or **to** their measurements.

gloss: To press clothes smooth with a hot iron.
examples: I *iron* my shirts on Sunday night.
She *ironed* the collar flat and hung the shirt up.
He was *ironing* when the doorbell rang.
contrast: The *r* is said before the vowel: EYE-urn, not eye-RON.

gloss: To make clothes smooth and flat with an iron, usually with steam.
examples: Could you *press* this shirt before the interview?
The hotel *pressed* his suit overnight.
Her uniform was freshly *pressed*.

gloss: To take wrinkles out of cloth with hot vapor.
examples: *Steam* the dress instead of ironing it.
She *steamed* the suit in the bathroom while the shower ran.
The gown is being *steamed* right now.

gloss: To stiffen cloth with starch so that it holds its shape.
examples: The cleaners *starch* his collars every week.
She *starched* the tablecloth until it stood up on its own.
He wore a heavily *starched* white shirt.

gloss: To get small folds and creases in cloth, or to put them there.
examples: Linen *wrinkles* if you look at it.
The shirt *wrinkled* badly in the suitcase.
He showed up in a *wrinkled* jacket.
contrast: The *w* is silent: RING-kuhl.

gloss: To press a sharp line into cloth, or to get an unwanted fold in it.
examples: Marines *crease* their trousers razor sharp.
He *creased* the slacks down the front.
Her dress was badly *creased* after the flight.

gloss: To flatten cloth with your hands.
examples: *Smooth* the fabric before you pin it.
She *smoothed* her skirt and sat down.
He was *smoothing* his tie against his chest.
contrast: The *th* is voiced, as in *this*. The verb is spelled *smooth*, never smoothe.

gloss: To wash and iron clothes or linens.
examples: The hotel *launders* the sheets daily.
She *laundered* the uniforms over the weekend.
His shirts came back freshly *laundered*.
contrast: *Launder* is the formal word; at home Americans say *do the laundry* or just *wash*.

gloss: To clean clothes with water and soap.
examples: *Wash* dark colors separately.
She *washed* the sweater by hand in cold water.
That shirt has been *washed* so many times it is gray.
contrast: The American vowel is /ɑː/: WAHSH. The third person adds *-es*: *washes*.

gloss: To leave cloth in water for a long time, usually to loosen a stain.
examples: *Soak* it in cold water, never hot.
She *soaked* the shirt overnight.
The tablecloth is still *soaking* in the sink.

gloss: To wash the soap out of cloth with clean water.
examples: *Rinse* the wool twice and press the water out.
He *rinsed* his socks in the hotel sink.
The towels have been *rinsed* but not dried.

gloss: To make something dry, or to become dry.
examples: Wool sweaters *dry* flat, never on a hanger.
She *dried* the jeans on the line.
My jacket is still *drying* by the radiator.
contrast: The *y* becomes *i*: *dry → dries, dried*, but *drying* keeps the *y*.

gloss: To make cloth white or lighter with a chemical.
examples: Never *bleach* colored cotton.
He *bleached* the towels and ruined two of them.
Her jeans have been *bleached* almost white.

gloss: To make something slightly wet.
examples: *Dampen* the cloth before you press the seam.
She *dampened* the collar and ironed it flat.
He is *dampening* the shirt with a spray bottle.

gloss: To put a chemical on cloth to protect it or to remove a stain.
examples: *Treat* the spot before it dries.
She *treated* the collar with stain remover.
The fabric has been *treated* to resist water.

gloss: To rub something hard with a brush or cloth to get it clean.
examples: *Scrub* the collar with a little soap first.
He *scrubbed* the grass stain out of her jeans.
She was *scrubbing* the cuffs by hand.
contrast: The *b* doubles: *scrub → scrubbed, scrubbing*.

gloss: To bend clothes or cloth neatly over on themselves.
examples: I will *fold* the laundry while you cook.
He *folded* the sweaters in threes.
The towels are *folded* and already put away.

gloss: To open out something that has been folded.
examples: *Unfold* the shirt carefully so it does not wrinkle.
She *unfolded* the dress and hung it by the window.
The napkin had been *unfolded* and left on the chair.

gloss: To put clothes into a bag or a suitcase for a trip.
examples: *Pack* light, one pair of shoes at most.
She *packed* three sweaters and wore none of them.
He is *packing* for a week in Chicago.

gloss: To take things out of a bag or a suitcase.
examples: *Unpack* tonight or everything will be wrinkled.
He *unpacked* and hung up his suit.
She has already *unpacked* both bags.

gloss: To put things into groups by type or color.
examples: *Sort* the whites from the colors before you start.
He *sorted* the socks into pairs.
She is *sorting* winter clothes from summer ones.

ru: подбирать в пару, сочетать, сочетать с
gloss: To put two things together, or to wear one item with another.
examples: *Pair* the gray blazer with dark jeans.
She *paired* the socks as she folded them.
That skirt is usually *paired* with boots.
contrast: You pair one thing **with** another. *Pair*, *pear* the fruit, and *pare* meaning to peel all sound alike.

gloss: To put clothes away safely until they are needed again.
examples: *Store* wool with cedar to keep the moths out.
She *stored* the winter coats in the attic.
The dresses are *stored* in cloth bags.

gloss: To arrange things in a tidy, useful order.
examples: I need to *organize* my closet this weekend.
He *organized* his shirts by color.
She spent Saturday *organizing* the kids' drawers.
contrast: American spelling takes *-ize*; British writing often has *organise*.

gloss: To turn cloth into a tube shape, or to turn a sleeve or cuff upward in folds.
examples: *Roll* your shirts instead of folding them and they will fit.
He *rolled* his sleeves to the elbow.
Her jeans were *rolled* at the ankle.

gloss: To divide things into groups, or to keep them apart.
examples: *Separate* the whites from the darks.
She *separated* the wool items before washing.
The delicates are *separated* into a mesh bag.
contrast: The verb ends in /eɪt/, SEP-uh-rayt; the adjective *separate* is SEP-rit. There is an *a* in the middle: sep-**a**-rate.

gloss: To look right together, or to find something that goes with something else.
examples: Those shoes do not *match* the belt.
She *matched* the scarf to her coat.
They showed up in *matching* sweaters.
contrast: The third person adds *-es*: *matches*. You match one thing **to** or **with** another.

gloss: To look bad together, especially two colors or patterns.
examples: Orange and pink *clash*, but she wears them anyway.
The tie *clashed* with his shirt.
Those two patterns are *clashing* badly.
contrast: One color clashes **with** another.

gloss: To go well with something and make it look better.
examples: A gray tie would *complement* that suit.
The blue scarf *complemented* her eyes.
The pieces were chosen to be *complemented* by simple jewelry.
contrast: *Complement*, with an *e*, means goes well with. *Compliment*, with an *i*, means kind words. They sound the same.

gloss: To tell someone that you like something about them.
examples: Three people *complimented* my coat today.
She *compliments* his taste every time he wears it.
He was *complimented* on the suit all evening.
contrast: You compliment someone **on** something. Do not mix it up with *complement*, spelled with an *e*.

ru: сочетать, подбирать по цвету и стилю
gloss: To choose clothes or colors that go together well.
examples: She can *coordinate* colors better than anyone I know.
They *coordinated* their outfits for the photo.
His shoes and belt are perfectly *coordinated*.
contrast: The verb ends in /eɪt/, koh-OR-duh-nayt; the noun *coordinate* ends in a schwa, koh-OR-duh-nut.

gloss: To be clearly different from something beside it, or to set two things side by side to show the difference.
examples: White stitching *contrasts* nicely with black leather.
The designer *contrasted* heavy wool with thin silk.
A *contrasting* collar makes a plain shirt look custom.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, kuhn-TRAST; the noun is KAHN-trast. One thing contrasts **with** another.

gloss: To look good on a particular person, or to be right for them.
examples: That color really *suits* you.
The short haircut *suited* her.
He is not *suited* to a job with a dress code.
contrast: *Suit* means it looks good on you; *fit* means it is the right size. A jacket can fit and still not suit you.

gloss: To arrange clothes or hair to create a particular look.
examples: She can *style* one dress five different ways.
They *styled* the shoot in 1970s clothes.
His hair was *styled* for the photograph.

gloss: To wear clothes in order to show them to other people.
examples: Students *model* their own designs in the spring.
She *modeled* for a catalog one summer.
He is *modeling* the new uniform for the staff.
contrast: American keeps one *l*: *modeled, modeling*; British doubles it: *modelled*.

gloss: To hold a position so that someone can photograph or paint you.
examples: *Pose* by the window where the light is better.
They *posed* in their graduation gowns.
She was *posing* for the camera in her new coat.

gloss: To show something off openly so that everyone notices it.
examples: He likes to *flaunt* his expensive watches.
She *flaunted* the new boots all week.
They were *flaunting* their designer bags on the boardwalk.
contrast: *Flaunt*, to show off, is not *flout*, to break a rule openly.

gloss: To make someone look better than they usually do.
examples: That cut *flatters* almost everyone.
The dark blue *flattered* her.
It is not a *flattering* jacket on anyone.

gloss: To look at goods in a store without planning to buy anything.
examples: We are just going to *browse*.
She *browsed* the sale rack for an hour.
He was *browsing* the coats when the store closed.

gloss: To go to stores in order to buy things.
examples: I *shop* for shoes online now.
They *shopped* all afternoon and bought nothing.
She is *shopping* for a winter coat.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *shop → shopped, shopping*. You shop **for** something.

gloss: To make one feature more noticeable than the rest.
examples: A belt will *accentuate* your waist.
The dark trim *accentuated* his shoulders.
Her height was *accentuated* by the long coat.

gloss: To hide something so that it cannot be seen.
examples: A loose jacket will *conceal* the strap.
She *concealed* the stain with a scarf.
The zipper is *concealed* in the side seam.

gloss: To let something be seen that was covered before.
examples: The dress *reveals* one shoulder.
He took off his coat and *revealed* a bright orange sweater.
The curtain came back, *revealing* the wedding gown.

gloss: To put things where people can see them.
examples: They *display* the new coats in the front window.
The store *displayed* the dresses on antique mannequins.
Vintage hats were *displayed* along the whole wall.
contrast: A vowel comes before the *y*, so nothing changes: *displays, displayed*. Compare *try → tried*.

gloss: To get wider or longer with wear, or to pull cloth to make it bigger.
examples: These jeans *stretch* after an hour.
The sweater *stretched* out at the elbows.
The collar has been *stretched* out of shape.

gloss: To force yourself or something into a space that is barely big enough.
examples: I can still *squeeze* into my old suit.
She *squeezed* her feet into shoes a size too small.
He was *squeezing* three coats into one bag.
contrast: You squeeze **into** clothes that are too tight.

gloss: To hang down loosely because the shape is gone.
examples: Cheap knits *sag* at the knees.
The pockets *sagged* from all the keys he carried.
His jeans were *sagging* below his hips.
contrast: The *g* doubles: *sag → sagged, sagging*.

gloss: To press painfully on part of the body, as tight shoes do.
examples: These shoes *pinch* across the toes.
The new boots *pinched* until I broke them in.
The waistband was *pinching* all evening.

gloss: To rub the skin until it is sore.
examples: A wet collar will *chafe*.
The backpack strap *chafed* her shoulder.
His heels were *chafed* raw by the new boots.

gloss: To give the skin an unpleasant feeling that makes you want to scratch.
examples: Wool *itches* if you wear it against the skin.
The tag *itched* all day until I cut it out.
This sweater has been *itching* since I put it on.
contrast: The third person adds *-es*: *itches*.

gloss: To press against something and move, often wearing it out or making the skin sore.
examples: The heel *rubs* right here.
The strap *rubbed* a red mark on his neck.
The elbows have *rubbed* thin.
contrast: The *b* doubles: *rub → rubbed, rubbing*.

gloss: To pull at something with a short, sharp movement.
examples: Do not *tug* at the loose thread.
She *tugged* her skirt down as she stood up.
He kept *tugging* at his collar all through dinner.
contrast: The *g* doubles: *tug → tugged, tugging*. You tug **at** something.

gloss: To hang low enough to touch the ground, or to pull something along it.
examples: The hem *drags* on the floor without heels.
Her coat *dragged* through the slush.
The gown was so long that it was *dragging* behind her.
contrast: The *g* doubles: *drag → dragged, dragging*. There is no form draggeed or drug in standard writing.

gloss: To move loosely back and forth in the air.
examples: Loose shirts *flap* in this wind.
His open coat *flapped* as he ran for the bus.
The laundry was *flapping* on the line.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *flap → flapped, flapping*.

gloss: To take something you bought back to the store.
examples: You can *return* it within thirty days with the receipt.
She *returned* the dress unworn.
These shoes have been *returned* twice.

gloss: To give something back and take a different one instead.
examples: Can I *exchange* this for a larger size?
He *exchanged* the sweater for the same one in blue.
The jacket was *exchanged* without any trouble.
contrast: You exchange one thing **for** another.

gloss: To give clothes or money away to a charity.
examples: We *donate* whatever the kids grow out of.
She *donated* six bags of clothes.
The coats were *donated* to a shelter downtown.

ru: брать на время, одалживать, одолжить (у кого-то)
gloss: To take something that belongs to someone else and give it back later.
examples: Can I *borrow* your black tie?
She *borrowed* her sister's dress for the wedding.
He has *borrowed* that jacket three times now.
contrast: You borrow something **from** a person; that person *lends* it **to** you.

gloss: To clean or smooth something with a brush.
examples: *Brush* the coat before you hang it up.
He *brushed* the lint off his shoulders.
She is *brushing* the dried mud off her boots.

gloss: To give one thing and get another in return.
examples: They *swap* sweaters all the time.
She *swapped* her scarf for his gloves.
The two sizes had been *swapped* by mistake.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *swap → swapped, swapping*.

gloss: To push things into a small space without much care.
examples: Do not *stuff* your coat into the locker.
He *stuffed* his gloves into his pockets.
The closet was *stuffed* with clothes she never wore.

gloss: To add decoration to something plain.
examples: They *embellish* the jackets with beads by hand.
She *embellished* a plain dress with ribbon.
The collar is *embellished* with tiny crystals.

gloss: To treat something so that water cannot get through it.
examples: *Waterproof* your boots before the first snow.
He *waterproofed* the jacket with a spray.
The seams have been *waterproofed* at the factory.

gloss: To receive something from an older member of the family.
examples: Younger brothers *inherit* everything in this house.
She *inherited* her grandmother's wool coat.
The ring had been *inherited* from his mother.
contrast: The *t* does not double, because the stress falls on the middle syllable: *inherited*, not inheritted.
